R062-01.notes: Passage explains the mechanism (setae, van der Waals, peeling release) and the research path (eliminating suction/glue/hooks, water-film test). A: author says synthetics do not yet match geckos; no prediction. C: no evolutionary history. D: glue/suction/hooks are only rejected hypotheses in para 1, not compared for strength.

R062-02.notes: Para 1: 'Glue was ruled out because gecko feet have no glands that secrete anything sticky.' A is the reason against suction; B is the reason against hooks; C is the water-film test from para 3.

R062-03.notes: Para 3: 'If water films were essential, the setae should have gripped the water-attracting surfaces far more strongly.' A is what the actual (similar-grip) result supported. B: humidity not tested by this experiment, and a stronger grip on water-attracting surfaces would suggest water matters, the opposite. D: rough vs. smooth was not tested.

R062-04.notes: The 'though' clause qualifies the van der Waals conclusion: water/humidity adds 'somewhat'. B: the clause still calls van der Waals 'the main source', so nothing was disproved. C: nothing about geckos avoiding dry places. D: release is introduced in para 4, not by this clause.

R062-05.notes: 'Any single contact is feeble, but billions...produce a grip strong' sets feeble against strong, so it means weak. A and C are senses that apply to people, not to forces. B is the sense used for arguments; nothing is being argued here.

R062-06.notes: Tape 'comes off more easily when pulled from one edge', just as setae 'peel away...a few at a time'. 'Far less force' is a fair paraphrase of 'more easily' together with 'almost absent'. A: para 1 says there is no sticky secretion, and the analogy is about how things peel off, not what they are made of. C: losing grip after many steps is not the point here (the last paragraph says geckos keep working). D: no strip arrangement is mentioned.

R062-07.notes: Adhesion depends on the branches getting 'extremely close' to the surface so van der Waals forces can act, so a surface they cannot approach closely would weaken the grip. B: the grip was similar on water-repelling surfaces. C: geckos cling to polished glass. D: geckos still clung in a vacuum.

R062-08.notes: Para 3: 'Some researchers suspected that thin films of water...were doing the work through capillary attraction.' A and B were obvious guesses already ruled out in para 1, before van der Waals was proposed, so they were not alternatives to it. D: electric charge is never mentioned.

R062-09.notes: Synthetics 'can now hold heavy objects...and release them cleanly, though none yet matches' the gecko's ability to stay clean and keep working. A contradicts 'hold heavy objects'. B contradicts 'none yet matches'. C: the synthetics copy gecko feet, so they are directly related.

R062-10.notes: Para 4: 'When a gecko curls its toes upward, the setae peel away from the surface a few at a time.' B: there are no secretions (para 1). C: release depends on angle, not on the forces weakening by themselves. D: pulling straight out is the hard way, as with tape.
